power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Behavioural decision science aspires to both explain human behaviour and improve real-world outcomes.
Yet despite a wealth of empirical support for decision theories, its impact has often fallen short.
We argue that this shortfall stems partly from underspecified theories and overly task-specific models that limit generalisability.
To do so, we revisit the conceptual foundations of modelling in decisionmaking research and propose a framework clarifying the relationship between theories and models.

We contrast theory-driven with emerging data-driven approaches, such as neural networks, which prioritise predictive accuracy but offer limited explanatory insight and deepen ethical concerns raised by model-based interventions.

Rather than viewing theory-and data-driven approaches as mutually exclusive, we advocate for synergistic integration: data-driven tools can support theory refinement and the piloting of applications, while the presence of explicit theories preserves interpretability.
Greater epistemological clarity can foster progress in both understanding behaviour and designing interventions to change it.
"Almost all our major problems involve human behavior, and they cannot be solved by physical and biological technology alone.
What is needed is a technology of behavior […].
Skinner's remark states one of the goals of behavioural science: to use our understanding of human behaviour to advance health and well-being in everyday life 1 .

text.text: The value of a scientific theory is usually assessed along two dimensions: its epistemic value (its ability to explain observed behavioural phenomena) and its instrumental value (its capacity to predict and ultimately control future ones) 2 .

text.text: This applied aspect is especially prominent in decision science.

Choices about health, finance, education and social relationships accumulate over time into large and often unequal outcomes for individuals and societies, which makes decision-making a domain well suited to turning theories into applications that improve human welfare [3] [4] [5].
text.formatted: Choices about health, finance, education and social relationships accumulate over time into large and often unequal outcomes for individuals and societies, which makes decision-making a domain well suited to turning theories into applications that improve human welfare <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: To derive applications from theories, we need models, which serve as a formal interface between theory and specific situations.

To a first approximation, models differ from theories in specificity: they are models of something (a particular behavioural phenomenon in a specific context, such as choices among lotteries or in bandit tasks), whereas theories are general constructs meant to apply across a wide range of phenomena (e.g., prospect theory or reinforcement learning) 6 .

text.text: In recent years, almost every new study in behavioural decisionmaking has proposed a new model tailored to its task 7, 8 .

text.text: How much epistemic progress this proliferation of models has generated remains unclear, as does whether it brings us any closer to concrete applications 9, 10.

text.text: These theory-driven models remain the conventional approach in behavioural decision-making research, but no longer the only one.

Data-driven models, such as deep neural networks and, in particular, large language models, have gained prominence 11, 12 , together with online testing, large-scale data sharing and advances in deep learning.

text.text: They promise a new approach to decision science, and the enthusiasm they attract stems at least in part from dissatisfaction with the standard approach, including doubts about the capacity of theory-driven models to consistently deliver useful applications 13.

text.text: This shift raises two critical questions.

First, what are the epistemological weaknesses of the standard, theory-driven modelling approach in decision-making Glossary Framework: a general description of the structure of the world that provides the language and conceptual basis in which theories are formulated 2 .

text.text: A framework is neither specified nor concretised, and sits above the theory-to-model transition analysed here; the research discussed in this article is almost entirely formulated within a single, computational framework.
Theory: a set of principles that posits relationships between variables or processes and encompasses a broad domain of application.
In behavioral decision-making framework, theories are generally underspecified with respect to functional form and parameter values and cannot, by themselves, be directly simulated.
A theory becomes a model not by being further specified, but by being concretised: tied to a particular application case.
Theory-driven Model: a specific instantiation of a theory in which functional forms, variables and parameter values are sufficiently specified to generate predictions for a defined empirical context.
A model serves as the formal interface between theory and data and can be simulated and empirically tested.
A theory becomes a model not by being further specified, but by being concretised: tied to a particular application case.
Data-driven model: a model whose structure is primarily derived from statistical regularities in data rather than from prior theoretical commitments about underlying mechanisms.
Such models often prioritise predictive performance over interpretability.
Parameter: a quantitative element of a model that modulates the strength, rate or shape of a computational process (for example, a learning rate or loss-aversion coefficient).
Parameters constrain model behaviour but in behavioral decision-making they are often estimated from data rather than fixed a priori.
Fitting: the procedure by which parameter values are estimated so as to optimise a model's correspondence with observed data, typically by maximising likelihood or minimising error.
This process often characterizes the final step of concretization in theory-driven models.

Training: the process by which a data-driven model adjusts its internal parameters through exposure to data in order to optimise a predefined objective function (typically, out-of-sample prediction accuracy).
Specification: the process of progressively increasing theoretical commitment by moving from broad relational statements to more detailed computational and functional formulations.
Concretisation: the step by which a theory, at whatever degree of specification, is adapted to a particular empirical context by instantiating task-specific variables and constraints.
Concretisation is specific to a given phenomenon (often materialised as a decision-making task in behavioural decision-making research).
Explanation: an account of a phenomenon that identifies the underlying mechanisms or principles responsible for generating it.
In behavioural decision-making, explanation typically involves being able to 'spell out' the theoretical principles underlying observed decision-making patterns.
Prediction: the generation of expected outcomes or behaviours in new observations based on a model.
Predictive success refers to the accuracy of these forecasts, preferably out-of-sample.
Generalisation: the extent to which a model's explanatory and predictive performance extends beyond the specific context, task or dataset on which it was developed.
Generalisation reflects robustness across variations in environments, populations or problem structures.
Application: the use of scientific findings to inform, design or implement interventions in real-world contexts (for example, clinical, economic or educational settings).
Behavioural intervention: a modification of the environment, made by a designer, that aims to change the behaviour of a target.
The interventions considered here rest on behavioural findings.

They are theory-driven when these findings have been used to infer a theory from which the intervention is designed, and data-driven when the findings are used to design the intervention directly, without an intermediate theory.

To address these questions, this paper delves into an analysis of the relationship between theories and models.
We start by identifying critical challenges and checkpoints in the standard approach.
Next, we explore how the standard theory-to-model transition framework relates to the new class of data-driven decision-making models.

Finally, we examine the implications for the translation of behavioural findings into real-life applications, pointing to critical steps of the theory-to-model transition that constitute obstacles in the transition from theory to practice, and to the ethical questions that translation raises whichever kind of model is used.
Of note, we do not review the record of behavioural interventions in any specific applied domain; we ask what in the standard modelling pipeline makes that record hard to improve.
Developing and validating robust theories and models are considered to be the primary goals of the scientific endeavour 13, 14 .

This lack of consensus is not exclusive to behavioural decisionmaking science; it has also proven difficult to achieve agreement among philosophers and scientists in other fields 2, 9, 14.

text.text: An example from physics illustrates the distinction.

Newton's theory of gravitation states that the attractive force between two bodies is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance, scaled by a universal gravitational constant.
By itself, the theory is not a model of any particular phenomenon.

It becomes one, say of the solar system or of the Galilean satellites of Jupiter, when its variables (e.g., masses and distances) are given concrete, empirical values; the model can then (retrospectively) explain observed planetary trajectories and (prospectively) predict future positions.
Understanding this theory-to-model transition in the context of behavioural decision-making research is considerably less straightforward than in physics.

Our proposal considers that, while theories and models can be formulated with the same formal language, theories are hierarchically superior latent constructs from which models are derived, and models are specific instantiations of a theory that allow it to be empirically tested 2 (see Glossary, Framework).
Models are typically derived from theories in two steps.
The first, specification, moves from general statements of principle to more detailed computational instantiations of specific phenomena (Figure 1a,b).
text.formatted: The first, specification, moves from general statements of principle to more detailed computational instantiations of specific phenomena (Figure <ref type="figure">1a</ref>,<ref type="figure">b</ref>).

text.text: We reject the common view that this gradient of specification simply maps onto the distinction between verbal theories and theories expressed in computational or mathematical terms 18 .
text.formatted: We reject the common view that this gradient of specification simply maps onto the distinction between verbal theories and theories expressed in computational or mathematical terms <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: The two often coincide in practice, but nothing prevents a computationally specified theory from being formulated verbally, for instance when its equations are described in natural language.
Conversely, a high-level theory can be expressed mathemat-ically using basic operators (such as proportionality) or relations (such as monotonicity), before committing to a specific functional form.

To illustrate, consider a broad statement, central to learning and decision-making, inspired by Thorndike's law of effect 19 (Figure 1b): "actions followed by satisfaction tend to be repeated" This statement minimally fulfils a theory's function: it explains why actions are repeated ("because they have been followed by satisfaction") and predicts future actions (assuming we know whether they will be followed by satisfaction).
text.formatted: To illustrate, consider a broad statement, central to learning and decision-making, inspired by Thorndike's law of effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> (Figure <ref type="figure">1b</ref>): "actions followed by satisfaction tend to be repeated" This statement minimally fulfils a theory's function: it explains why actions are repeated ("because they have been followed by satisfaction") and predicts future actions (assuming we know whether they will be followed by satisfaction).

text.text: It can therefore be considered a theory of decision-making (and, in fact, it has been 19 ).
text.formatted: It can therefore be considered a theory of decision-making (and, in fact, it has been <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> ).

text.text: Its formulation, however, is broad: while it prescribes a directionality between its core elements (action and satisfaction), it leaves out many potentially important details of the underlying computational processes.

A further step of specification commits to the computational details of the process and to the theory's components, for example 20 : "After a reward is obtained, it is used to update the internal estimate of the subjective value of an option via a prediction error minimization mechanism.
text.formatted: A further step of specification commits to the computational details of the process and to the theory's components, for example <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> : "After a reward is obtained, it is used to update the internal estimate of the subjective value of an option via a prediction error minimization mechanism.

text.text: When the option is encountered again, this subjective value will be fed into a stochastic selection process that generates actions with a probability that is a sigmoid function of their subjective values".

This second statement is fully compatible with the previous one, provided that satisfaction is understood in relative terms (as an outcome better than expected, a reading that the original formulation does not preclude) 21 .
text.formatted: This second statement is fully compatible with the previous one, provided that satisfaction is understood in relative terms (as an outcome better than expected, a reading that the original formulation does not preclude) <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: It clearly contains more detail regarding the computational steps involved in generating the behavioural phenomenon of interest.

Moreover, especially when expressed in terms of equations or code, the elements of the theory become more focused and concrete, for example "satisfaction" is now formalized as a numerical reward, and actions are treated as discrete choices.
At this stage, we see a commitment to a specific functional form: the statement explicitly points to a delta rule for updating and a softmax function for choice selection, respectively.

text.text: This phrase, commonly used to describe loss aversion, a cornerstone of prospect theory, conveys that the subjective value of losses exceeds that of equivalent gains, but not how, by how much, or in which contexts.

Compare: "When making decisions under risk, the magnitude of a loss is subjectively perceived as greater than that of a gain of comparable magnitude-as if it were multiplied by a factor greater than one" This second formulation commits more clearly to a functional form and to the relevant elements (such as outcome magnitudes).
In both cases, however, specification remains incomplete: functional forms are governed by parameters whose values have not yet been defined.

Parameter definition, here setting the learning rate or the loss aversion coefficient within defined priors, typically comes at the end of specification (we return below to how this may complicate the translation of cognitive theories into real-life applications).
The process of concretization allows a theory about a general cognitive process to become a model of a specific empirical phenomenon (Figure 1a,b).
text.formatted: The process of concretization allows a theory about a general cognitive process to become a model of a specific empirical phenomenon (Figure <ref type="figure">1a</ref>,<ref type="figure">b</ref>).

text.text: Theories are typically proposed and understood as abstract descriptions of broad mechanisms with relatively wide domains of application (e.g., learning from reward, or making decisions under risk and loss).

For example, a model derived from the learning theory described above would need to be adapted to reflect the specifics of an experimental setting: the number of options presented to participants, the magnitude and frequency of rewards, the number of trials, and so on.

In practice, a model is the adaptation of a computational theory to a particular situation (application case) 2 , which, in the context of behavioural decision-making research, typically corresponds to the task used to elicit choices.
First, in our framework, specification is a gradient that runs across both theories and models.
At one end of this spectrum lie relatively broad relational statements, and at the other, clearly formulated functional forms with explicit computational parameterisation.

Crucially, position on this gradient is not what distinguishes a theory from a model: that distinction is carried by concretisation, which is not a matter of degree, since a model is always a model of a specific application case.
Specification and concretisation are therefore largely orthogonal, which is why Figure 1a,b represents them as two separate steps.
text.formatted: Specification and concretisation are therefore largely orthogonal, which is why Figure <ref type="figure">1a</ref>,b represents them as two separate steps.

text.text: Second, multiple models can be devised as distinct instantiations of the same theory.

This reflects the fact that a single theory can be used to generate different models tailored to different contexts or situations, which, in the laboratory, often translates into different behavioural tasks.
The range of phenomena that a theory can account for depends on the breadth of its domain of application.
A model can therefore be simulated, whereas a theory, a broad statement about a cognitive process not yet tied to any specific application, cannot.
This also implies a gradient in falsifiability.

A high-level theory without specific computational details is comparatively difficult to falsify (one can conceive of the law of effect being false, but its lack of specification makes it hard to design a decisive experiment).
In contrast, a fully parametrized model can be more readily falsified, especially when its domain of application is narrowly defined and its behaviour is tightly constrained by its parameterization.

Decomposing the theory-to-model transition into specification and concretisation yields an operational epistemological pipeline, and makes explicit two critical challenges for behavioural decision-making research.
The first is the lack of clarity about the stage of specification at which concretisation, the adaptation of a theory to a specific empirical application, should occur.
Consider again Newton's theory of gravitation (Figure 1a).
text.formatted: Consider again Newton's theory of gravitation (Figure <ref type="figure">1a</ref>).

text.text: The theory comes fully specified, with both a welldefined functional form and parameterization (e.g., the universal gravitational constant, itself determined empirically, but whose successive measurements refine a single value used in every application of the theory).
Concretisation occurs after full specification, when the function is fed the masses and distances of the relevant bodies, yielding models of particular gravitational systems (e.g., the solar system).

The theory itself is both rigid (fixed functional form and parameters) and general (applicable as it is to many different situations); it is the rigidity of these commitments, not their absence, that gives the theory its strength.

In contrast, theories in behavioural decision-making, such as reinforcement learning or prospect theory, are often confronted with data while still under-specified, particularly in their parameters, whose values are standardly estimated by fitting.
Theoretical commitments in our field are often much weaker than in other natural sciences.

Frequently, the only rigid aspect of a theory is its functional form, which effectively leaves fitting to determine key steps of its specification (and sometimes even the functional form is selected on empirical performance) 8, 16 .
text.formatted: Frequently, the only rigid aspect of a theory is its functional form, which effectively leaves fitting to determine key steps of its specification (and sometimes even the functional form is selected on empirical performance) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: Fitted parameter ranges sometimes exceed the bounds implied by the theory's core commitments (e.g., a loss aversion coefficient below one, contradicting the tenet that "losses loom larger than gains").

A behavioural scientist will far more readily commit to the theory that "value is updated using a temporal difference rule" than to the theory that "value is updated using a temporal difference rule with a learning rate of 0.34" 24 .

text.text: This reluctance yields "weak" theories, too flexible to impose strong constraints on the phenomena they aim to explain 25.

text.text: The framework also helps to assess the theoretical contribution of a given study.

Modelling papers in decision science typically introduce a new task, fit several models to the resulting data and declare a "winning" model, rejecting the "losing" ones (how such adjudication should be performed is a separate question 16, 17 ).
text.formatted: Modelling papers in decision science typically introduce a new task, fit several models to the resulting data and declare a "winning" model, rejecting the "losing" ones (how such adjudication should be performed is a separate question <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> ).

text.text: The winner is generally taken as theoretical progress; attending to specification and concretisation shows more precisely how much progress was made.

Compare a reinforcement learning study contrasting models derived from competing theories, one positing that outcome values are represented on a relative scale and the other on an absolute scale 21 , with a study contrasting two models of relative outcome encoding, one following a divisive and the other a range normalization rule 26 .
text.formatted: Compare a reinforcement learning study contrasting models derived from competing theories, one positing that outcome values are represented on a relative scale and the other on an absolute scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> , with a study contrasting two models of relative outcome encoding, one following a divisive and the other a range normalization rule <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: The first advance intuitively appears more substantial, and the framework explains why: the first comparison operates at the level of broad theoretical commitments (low specification), the second at the level of functional form within a shared theory (high specification).

That concretisation typically occurs at an incomplete level of specification, with parameters defined only once a model is fitted to data, interacts with another problem: in behavioural decision-making, parameters are not universal but are likely influenced by the situation in which the decision process is deployed.
In the gravity example, the only parameter is the gravitational constant (G = 6.6743 × 10 -11 ), literally a universal constant, assumed to take the same value at all times and places.

By contrast, parameters such as learning rates or loss aversion coefficients vary (Figure 1c), not only because of underlying inter-individual differences (genetic or developmental) but also because different situations (in practice, different behavioural tasks) elicit genuinely different parameter values 27, 28 .

text.text: This suggests that the limited theoretical commitment at the specification stage is not merely a consequence of current practice (waiting to fix parameters until model fitting) but also reflects an intrinsic constraint on behavioural decisionmaking (and perhaps cognitive science) theories: the phenomena they seek to explain are intrinsically variable, so they lack an equivalent of universal constants.
Scientific progress is not only measured by the development of increasingly accurate theories and models, but also by their capacity to improve real-world outcomes.

In this respect, behavioural decision-making science, despite producing a proliferation of theories and models, some of which span multiple levels of description and explain laboratory findings well (e.g., reinforcement learning or prospect theory), has generally fallen short of expectations when it comes to delivering ro-bust real-life applications, in computational psychiatry and behavioural policy alike.
This lack of translation is worth dwelling on not only because it limits societal impact, but also because it may reflect deeper epistemological issues 2, 5, [29] [30] [31] [32].

text.text: In light of our framework, the direct translation of fully specified models into real-life applications is unlikely to be fruitful, for two main reasons.
First, laboratory models are typically built on tasks that present decision problems in extremely controlled, and to some extent aseptic, formats 33 .
text.formatted: First, laboratory models are typically built on tasks that present decision problems in extremely controlled, and to some extent aseptic, formats <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> .

text.text: Such designs isolate key cognitive processes and minimise confounds, but they strip away much of the complexity of real-life decisions, which rarely occur in isolation and in which contextual confounds are the rule, not the exception.
Reinforcement learning, for instance, rests largely on two-(or few-) alternative forced-choice paradigms.

These neglect at least two features systematically present in real-life decisions: the cost of making a choice (often negligible in the laboratory, where choices are easy and forced) and the option of deferring or avoiding a decision altogether 34 .
text.formatted: These neglect at least two features systematically present in real-life decisions: the cost of making a choice (often negligible in the laboratory, where choices are easy and forced) and the option of deferring or avoiding a decision altogether <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> .

text.text: Laboratory tasks also typically use secondary, contrived or extrinsic rewards, whereas much of everyday behaviour is driven by intrinsic goals.
More generally, the goals of the experiment and those of the participants are aligned mainly through written instructions, a tenuous link that participants often overlook [35] [36] [37].
text.formatted: More generally, the goals of the experiment and those of the participants are aligned mainly through written instructions, a tenuous link that participants often overlook <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: The second reason is that humans exhibit computational plasticity (or meta-learning) 38, 39 : the brain tunes its learning and decision-making parameters to the context and to experience.
text.formatted: The second reason is that humans exhibit computational plasticity (or meta-learning) <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> : the brain tunes its learning and decision-making parameters to the context and to experience.

text.text: Until we are able to fully capture and model these meta-learning and contextual processes, we will necessarily be dealing with situation-specific models, which depend on data for their parameter values.
Meta-learning adds to genuine inter-individual differences of genetic or ontogenetic origin and to developmental or environmental fluctuations [40] [41] [42] .

text.text: Research has therefore increasingly turned to models that prioritise predictive performance over theoretical elegance and interpretability.

A first explicit step toward this prediction-first approach was the choice prediction competition, inspired by large-scale machine learning benchmarks such as the ImageNet visual recognition challenge 43, 49, 50 : a large dataset of human decisions is released, research groups train their predictive models on it, and performance is evaluated on a separate test dataset.

text.text: A key ingredient, argued to improve on theorydriven approaches, is the diversity of the training data: to avoid overfitting the functional form and parameters to one task design, the dataset must encompass a wide range of decision problems.

In practice, however, the problems used in these competitions have themselves remained relatively abstract, which limits what their predictive success establishes about generalisation beyond the laboratory.

Deep neural networks took the prediction-first approach further, delegating model design from researchers to the optimisation process itself, which adjusts model weights to maximise choice prediction accuracy (Figure 2a).

text.text: The essential difference lies in what these models represent.

Theory-driven models are derived from general principles and aim to explain latent cognitive processes; neural network models capture statistical regularities in the data: they are, in effect, models of the dataset.

Given their data-intensive training and flexibility, such models may well predict accurately and even generalise across tasks or domains (although this remains to be formally demonstrated 56 ), which would be especially useful for real-world applications.

Data-driven approaches are usually characterised by the amount of data they require.
Quantity is, however, only one of three dimensions along which datasets differ.
The first is quantity: data-driven models generally require more observations than theory-driven ones, because their structure is estimated from the data.
The second is source.

Laboratory data come from tasks designed by researchers, whether administered in person or online; ecological data are produced by behaviour outside the laboratory, such as social media activity, food-delivery orders or purchase records [71] [72] [73] [74] 84 .

text.text: The third is diversity: a dataset may consist of many repetitions of similar decision problems, or of varied problems drawn from different paradigms.

The distinction matters because the two promises of data-driven approaches lie in different regions.

Theory discovery, as in scientific regret minimisation 75 , is best served by large quantities of uniform, well-controlled data: enough observations of the same problem to locate where a standard model fails, and to let a flexible model identify what is missing.

A dataset well suited to one purpose may therefore be poorly suited to the other.

The two can nonetheless be combined in sequence: uniform data to specify a theory, by locating where it fails on a given problem, and diverse data to establish the range of situations over which the specified theory holds.

Data-driven models can be viewed as complex extensions of traditional statistical models.
In a typical reinforcement learning task, a temporal difference model that fits the observed choices qualitatively and quantitatively may be said to explain the behaviour.

A sufficiently flexible multiple regression, estimating the influence of previous outcomes on the probability of repeating a choice, might predict the same data even better; yet few would argue that it offers a meaningful explanation of the decision process.
By selecting models primarily on quantitative prediction, the data-driven approach may also overlook features of behaviour that are highly diagnostic of the underlying cognitive processes 57 .

text.text: Their lack of mechanistic explanation notwithstanding, one might argue that the putative superior predictive accuracy of data-driven models, and their datasetdriven capacity to generalise across decision-making contexts, make them valuable tools for translational research 11, 12, 43 .

text.text: This argument holds prima facie in applied domains such as policy design, economics, clinical practice or education, where anticipating behaviour is a prerequisite for designing effective interventions.
Here the lack of theoretical transparency introduces a translational barrier that is ethical rather than epistemological 61, 62 .
text.formatted: Here the lack of theoretical transparency introduces a translational barrier that is ethical rather than epistemological <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62</ref> .

text.text: The barrier is not opacity as such: medicine routinely and legitimately deploys effective treatments whose mechanisms are unknown, and what makes this acceptable is not mechanistic understanding but the regime that surrounds deployment, namely clinical trials establishing efficacy and safety beforehand, and monitoring for unintended consequences afterwards.

Behavioural interventions derived from opaque predictive models are at present deployed with nothing comparable in place, and the difficulty is not merely institutional: because the parameters of behavioural models are not universal constants, the domain within which a demonstration of efficacy transports is itself rarely established.
A further consideration is specific to our field.

A patient retains an independent standpoint from which to judge a treatment that acts on the body; an intervention designed to shift a choice acts on the very processes by which preferences are formed and decisions reached, and may succeed without the person being aware that their choice was shaped.

Many such interventions are opaque to their target, yet nudges inspired by prospect theory or behavioural therapies grounded in reinforcement learning can be explained and justified to the target individual, because their designer can state the regularity being exploited.
Where the underlying model is opaque, the designer cannot, and an intervention whose basis cannot be stated cannot be contested.

We therefore hold that model-derived behavioural interventions require both a staged regime of validation and post-deployment monitoring in which the domain of validity is explicitly assessed, and a higher standard of interpretability where the intervention targets choice itself.

text.text: The first is the replacement strategy, which assumes no coexistence is needed.
According to this view, due to their failure to yield robust applications or their limited domains of applicability, theory-driven models should be entirely replaced by data-driven ones 12 .
text.formatted: According to this view, due to their failure to yield robust applications or their limited domains of applicability, theory-driven models should be entirely replaced by data-driven ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: This position is typically advocated by application-oriented researchers who prioritize predictive performance over explanatory depth.
However, because datadriven models generally lack explanatory power, this strategy risks falling short of one of the main epistemic goals of scientific inquiry (explanation).

Furthermore, effectiveness alone does not justify the use of opaque models to design real-world interventions: such use requires a regime of validation that establishes the domain over which an intervention holds, and greater transparency where the intervention targets choice itself.
Opacity matters most where the model draws on sensitive personal data, such as age or gender, whose use must itself be justified.
A second option is the parallel strategy, which largely reflects the current state of affairs (with a few notable exceptions 76, 77, 83 ).
text.formatted: A second option is the parallel strategy, which largely reflects the current state of affairs (with a few notable exceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">76,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">77,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">83</ref> ).

text.text: In this model, theory-driven and data-driven approaches are pursued independently, often by different research groups, even when targeting the same or similar phenomena.
The downside of this arrangement is an unbounded proliferation of models: on the theory-driven side, a model for each task; on the data-driven side, a model for each dataset.
As science aims to reduce complexity, this fragmentation will prove epistemologically unsustainable in the long run.
Finally, the integrated strategy (see Figure 3b) seeks to leverage the strengths of both approaches.
text.formatted: Finally, the integrated strategy (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3b</ref>) seeks to leverage the strengths of both approaches.

text.text: In this view, while datadriven models are seen as epistemologically inferior to theorydriven models, they play a valuable role in theory development and application.
Small, interpretable data-driven models can help refine theories by identifying unexplained variance.

Recurrent networks with only a handful of hidden units, fitted to choice data, have proved simple enough to be analysed as dynamical systems, allowing candidate mechanisms to be read off them 76 ; and hybrid architectures that embed a trained network within an interpretable cognitive model have been used to revise specific hypotheses about the memory processes underlying reinforcement learning 77 .

text.text: What the approach demands is breadth of data: procedurally generated task spaces, and simulation from candidate generative processes, are plausible routes to supplying it.

Conversely, large, general-purpose data-driven models, such as fine-tuned LLMs, could in principle be used to stress-test the robustness and ecological validity of applications derived from theory, offering insight into whether those applications are likely to generalize beyond controlled laboratory contexts.

text.text: Our concern is that the pipeline described above tends to yield mechanisms whose scope is limited to narrow application cases: mechanism sketches, in which the conditions of validity are left unspecified 64 .

text.text: Conversely, even a correctly identified mechanism may support only weak predictions where behaviour is jointly produced by several generative processes, as it routinely is outside the laboratory.
Moreover, decision-making theories are often underspecified, and laboratory tasks give limited guidance for estimating parameters in ecological contexts.
How, then, can we develop models that better predict and boost decision-making outside the lab?
Several possible strategies are available.
First, we can improve the ecological validity of experimental tasks.
One promising direction is task gamification, which offers richer, more engaging environments while retaining experimental control 65, 66 .
text.formatted: One promising direction is task gamification, which offers richer, more engaging environments while retaining experimental control <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">66</ref> .

text.text: While the promise is strong, its ability to deliver better generalization beyond the lab still requires systematic validation; furthermore, consideration should be given as to whether gamification might create biases in data collection.
Second, we can try to estimate parameters directly from ecological data (broadly defined as data collected outside traditional lab settings 67 ).
text.formatted: Second, we can try to estimate parameters directly from ecological data (broadly defined as data collected outside traditional lab settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">67</ref> ).

text.text: This approach has been relatively successful in the context of prospect theory, although with high variability of parameter estimates [68] [69] [70] .

text.text: This approach is also gaining traction in other decision-making domains, including reinforcement learning research 71 .
text.formatted: This approach is also gaining traction in other decision-making domains, including reinforcement learning research <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">71</ref> .

text.text: Recent studies have fit RL models to online behaviours, such as food delivery choices or social media engagement [72] [73] [74] .

text.text: While encouraging, these efforts often reveal substantial discrepancies in parameter values compared to laboratory-based estimates, further underscoring the challenge of generalization and the need to refine theories, explaining the factors that influence such parameters, as work on adaptively set learning rates has attempted 38, 39.

text.text: Third, data-driven models offer an alternative route to generalization: by training on large, diverse datasets (including ecological data), they promise to learn behavioural regularities robust enough to generalize across tasks and domains.
This is the case that is made for such models; in our view their deployment must be weighed against the ethical and epistemological caveats highlighted above.
Moving forward, data-driven models, particularly neural networks, may still play a meaningful role in theory discovery and refinement.
For instance, Griffiths and colleagues have shown that such models can be used to estimate the upper bounds of learnable statistical regularities in a given task 75 .

text.text: Building on this perspective (Box 2; Figure 3a), we propose an integrated pipeline in which data-driven models are placed in the service of theory development and application (Figure 3b).

text.text: First, small and interpretable data-driven models can be fit to laboratory datasets and used to refine theory, by capturing behavioural variance that existing, top-down hypotheses do not account for.

The product of this step is a better-specified theory, not an application; whether the resulting theory supports better translation depends on the diversity, in terms of tasks and contexts, of the data on which it is then tested.

Breadth of data is not breadth of task, and existing demonstrations of this approach have used a comparatively narrow range of laboratory paradigms 76, 77 (Box 1); datasets should be selected for their coverage of the domain, not for what the current theory deems relevant (Box 2).

text.text: Once the revised theory has achieved sufficient coherence and explanatory power, it can serve as the basis for real-world applications.
Before these are deployed, large-scale data-driven models, such as finetuned large language models, could in principle stresstest their robustness and generalizability 80, 81 .

text.text: This, however, assumes that such models approximate human behaviour and preferences well across a wide range of settings, including ecological and less structured environments: an assumption that is contested and not currently established 56, 82 .

text.text: Data-driven models thus cannot (and should not) replace theory-driven models, but they can complement them 83 and contribute to theoretical progress (Box 2).

text.text: Finally, and perhaps most importantly, gaining epistemological clarity about the distinction between theories and models, and about the two key steps in the theory-to-model transition (specification and concretisation), is not merely a matter of terminological precision, a call for explicitness that has also been made in neighbouring fields 2 .
It is foundational for understanding how research in behavioural decision-making progresses, for diagnosing its limitations, and for directing future efforts.

Greater awareness of this framework within the scientific community could enhance conceptual coherence, foster more productive debates, and ultimately support the development of both better theories and more effective applications.
